Diagram titled "How a Context Language Model edits its context: A simple step-by-step view" outlining an 8-step process:
 * Start of turn: Current editable context exists in memory with old messages.
 * LLM reads the context: The LLM evaluates the context and decides to run a bash command to edit it.
 * Harness mirrors context: The harness mirrors the old editable context into a file at /tmp/.live_ctx/LIVE_CTX_MAIN.txt.
 * Bash command runs: The bash command executes and may edit that file.
 * Harness parses file: If the file changed, the harness parses it back into a new edited context.
 * Tool call appended: The current assistant tool call is appended to the edited context.
 * Tool result appended: The tool result is appended below the tool call.
 * Next turn starts: The next turn begins with the edited old context, previous tool call, and previous tool result.
Key idea box: "The model edits the prior context first. The tool call and tool result from the current turn are appended afterward, so they can only be compacted on the next turn."
Footer summary:
 * Ordinary LM: Context mostly grows by appending.
 * CLM: The model can rewrite the editable part of context between turns.

Quantum algorithmic optimization: Argon is helping our quantum computing researchers optimize the spacetime resources (qubits × gates) of subroutines that bottleneck important applications. In one example, it beat the published baseline by 40% in a matter of minutes.

    Memory efficiency: A team of Argon agents analyzed fleet-wide profiling telemetry to autonomously identify and apply memory optimizations across Google’s data centers, freeing up over 300 TiB of memory once rolled out, with an estimated 500 TiB to 1 PiB in total savings.

    Large Scale Codebase Migrations and Optimizations: Argon agents are working on migrating C/C++ codebases to Rust across Google—scaling from tens of thousands of lines in core libraries like re2, libgav1 up to 800K+ lines for the Fuchsia OS Zircon kernel. Given the criticality of many of these systems, such large-scale rewrites are undergoing rigorous automated and manual auditing, emulation testing, and review before rolling out to production.

Linguistically and cognitively, it is a textbook case of speech planning running completely off the rails—specifically a cascade of rapid false starts, lexical repair cycles, and syntactic abandonment (anacoluthon).
The speaker’s brain knows the general emotional weight of the idea it wants to convey, but the grammatical scaffolding collapses under real-time production pressure:
The Modal Search Loop: The speaker gets trapped in auxiliary-verb limbo (had → you’d → would → could → will → wants). In speech production theory, the message-level concept has arrived, but the grammatical encoder cannot decide which conditional frame to commit to—ability (could), desire (wants), or hypothetical action (would).
The Catastrophic Pronoun Drift: Midway through the reboot cycles, the thematic roles get swapped. It starts in the second person ("you could do") and abruptly mutates into an entirely different, third-person agent/patient structure ("you want him to do you so much").

It starts in the second person ("you could do") and abruptly mutates into an entirely different, third-person agent/patient structure ("you want him to do you so much"). The speaker likely tripped over a reference to an external figure (a hero, a character, or perhaps Hercules himself, given the original clip’s context) or conflated "something that makes you want to..." with "someone doing something for you."
The Structural Abandonment (Anacoluthon): The original framing ("Have you ever had a dream that...") requires a coherent relative or content clause to complete it. Instead of completing any of the six candidate clauses he opens, he abandons the grammar entirely and glides straight into an orphaned result clause: "...so much you could do anything?"

The Probable Target Thought
Stripped of the processing buffer and repair attempts, the intended sentence was almost certainly:
"Have you ever had a dream that you wanted [to come true] so much that you felt like you could do anything?"
The mouth started transmitting before the syntax had finished compiling, resulting in a loop where every failed attempt to self-correct introduced a new grammatical variable until he simply sprinted across the finish line.

Shun, David, Saul: signal

Shun and David have the same job: legitimating a throne that passes outside the father's line.
• Shun: Yao passes over his own son Danzhu and gives the throne to Shun, having already married him to his two daughters.
• David: Saul's daughter Michal marries David, and Jonathan cedes his claim freely: "thou shalt be king over Israel, and I shall be next unto thee" (1 Sam 23:17).
In both, the successor proves he isn't a usurper by being conspicuously loyal to the father who persecutes him. David spares Saul twice and calls him "my father" (1 Sam 24:11).

McCarter called the story of David's rise an apology, modeled on the Hittite Apology of Hattusili III, a usurper's self-justification.
Both traditions kept the counter-memory:
• Shimei curses David as a "man of blood" over Saul's house (2 Sam 16:7-8).
• The Bamboo Annals say Shun imprisoned Yao and kept Danzhu from seeing him, and Han Feizi says flatly that Shun coerced Yao.
